title: New Freddie Mercury Book Features Singer’s Personal Notes & Alternative ‘Bohemian Rhapsody’ Lyrics
summary: The latest book about the Queen frontman was created by his longtime friend, Mary Austin, based on the personal artifacts the singer left to her.
contentText:

Freddie Mercury left behind more than a legendary voice when he died in 1991. Now, a new book opens a window into the private creative world behind that legacy. A Life in Lyrics: The Official Creative Legacy of Freddie Mercury , published Sept. 1, 2026, depicts the Queen frontman’s life and songwriting through pages preserved by Mary Austin, his former fiancée and lifelong friend. The book brings together handwritten drafts, rough ideas, unused verses and visual notes from Mercury’s creative work, reaching from his pre-Queen days through his solo years.

Among the archive are early versions of “Bohemian Rhapsody” and several drafts connected to “Don’t Stop Me Now,” alongside complete songs that never made it into the studio. Personal photographs and recollections also add intimate context throughout the book. Available as a standard hardback , ebook and audiobook , the title also comes in a limited deluxe edition designed for collectors and devoted Queen fans alike.

This deluxe limited edition includes a slipcase with the first verse of “Bohemian Rhapsody” written in Mercury’s own handwriting, bespoke endpapers and four gatefolds featuring bonus “Bohemian Rhapsody” archive material and personal photographs.

Dey Street Books

Freddie Mercury ’s path to “Bohemian Rhapsody” began years before Queen recorded it, with fragments taking shape in the late 1960s. He worked from loose scraps and phone books, including an early idea known as “The Cowboy Song.” His vision eventually fused ballad, opera and hard rock.

Mercury kept the lyrics deliberately open, while some friends saw “Mama just killed a man” as a metaphor for leaving an old identity behind. According to the new book, the lyric was written when Mercury was still a student at Ealing Art College, and he saved it for years for the right song.

The standard hardback offers the core version of A Life in Lyrics at around one-fifth the deluxe price, making it an accessible collector’s item. The cover of the book features the opening lyrics of “Killer Queen” in Mercury’s own penmanship, making it a standout coffee-table display.

Another page devoted to “Killer Queen” inside captures Mercury’s restless pen at work. The song’s opening lyrics are surrounded by scribbles and doodles, turning the page into a snapshot of his creative habits rather than a polished manuscript. At the bottom, a later-looking addition, “Do you wanna try,” suggests the material remained open to revision even after the main writing was established.
